metadata.file_name: 129. Campos & Scherer. (2024). Digital gender gaps in Students’ knowledge, attitudes and skills: an integrative data analysis across 32 Countries.pdf
metadata.title: Digital gender gaps in Students’ knowledge, attitudes and skills: an integrative data analysis across 32 Countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 grade-8 student microdata under a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design (schools sampled with PPS, then 20 students sampled within schools). In stage 1, the authors estimate multigroup SEMs with complex sampling survey characteristics, explicitly incorporating sampling weights and jackknife/balanced repeated replication procedures, and they also incorporate plausible values for the digital skills outcomes. Missing data are handled via multiple imputation within each country and plausible-value-specific complete datasets, with parameter pooling using Rubin’s rules. In stage 2, the authors meta-analyze the resulting country-level direct and indirect effects using random- and mixed-effects models; the weighting logic is therefore embedded in the primary (country) effect-size generation rather than in a single pooled student-level ML model.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 grade-8 student data from 32 independent country samples that met eligibility criteria: K-12 student populations, gender information, at least one ICT-attitude measure, at least one performance-based digital competence measure, ICT access measure, representative random student samples, and coverage across multiple countries. The authors report that no countries or students were excluded from the final analyses; the analytic sample therefore includes all available students within the included ICILS country samples, with missing item/scale data handled via multiple imputation within each country.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2013 & 2018 Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) and Computational Thinking (CT)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Integrative data analysis via multigroup SEMs + random/multilevel meta-analysis. For ICT affect: direct effect (partially standardized) c′ps = -0.29 (95% CI [-0.35, -0.23]); indirect effect abps = 0.04 (95% CI [0.03, 0.06]). For ICT beliefs: positive attitudes direct effect c′ps = -0.13 (95% CI [-0.20, -0.07]); negative attitudes c′ps = -0.11 (95% CI [-0.16, -0.05]); future expectations c′ps = -0.12 (95% CI [-0.19, -0.04]); indirect effects near zero except positive attitudes abps = 0.04 (95% CI [0.02, 0.05]). For ICT self-efficacy: basic direct effect c′ps = -0.11 (95% CI [-0.15, -0.06]); advanced direct effect c′ps = -0.17 (95% CI [-0.22, -0.12]); indirect effects near zero (basic abps = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.07, -0.03]; advanced abps = 0.00, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.01]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2013 & 2018 Grade 8 the study leveraged ICT availability at home and students’ ICT attitudes (ICT affect, ICT beliefs, and ICT self-efficacy) to estimate direct and indirect gender effects on digital skills (CIL/CT), finding that girls outperform boys in digital skills with moderate negative direct effects (e.g., c′ps = -0.29 via ICT affect) and that attitudes toward technology partially mediate the gender gap (e.g., positive indirect effect via ICT affect; indirect effects near zero for several belief/self-efficacy subdimensions). This indicates that gender-equity interventions should target students’ technology attitudes—especially affect/interest and positive attitudes—rather than focusing only on access to ICT.

data.outcome_summary: This integrative data analysis synthesizes individual participant data from ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 for grade-8 students across 32 country samples (total N = 105,981). The authors generate country-specific direct and indirect effects of gender on digital skills (CIL in both cycles; CT in 2018) using multigroup SEMs with complex survey design features, plausible values, and multiple imputation, then combine effect sizes via multivariate random- and multilevel meta-analysis. Across attitude dimensions, girls show moderate advantages in digital skills after controlling for ICT access and attitudes (e.g., direct effect via ICT affect c′ps = -0.29, 95% CI [-0.35, -0.23]). Mediation is strongest for ICT affect (indirect effect abps = 0.04, 95% CI [0.03, 0.06]) and weaker/near zero for several belief and self-efficacy subdimensions. Limitations include reliance on cross-sectional ICILS measures and the fact that the analysis estimates associations/mediation within a modeling framework rather than causal effects.
